lessons.title: What Claude Is Actually Good At
lessons.subtitle: A capability map, not a marketing brochure

blocks.md: Most people use Claude the way they use Google in 2009: they type a question and hope. That works for trivia, and it fails for everything else. The first thing you have to internalise is that Claude is **not a search engine, not an oracle, and not a coworker who has read your docs**. Claude is a fast, articulate junior with infinite patience, no memory between sessions, and a worrying willingness to make things up when it has no source. This lesson is the picture you should hold the next time you open the chat.

blocks.title: Mental model: Claude is a fast junior with infinite patience
blocks.md:
Picture the most willing junior on your team. They have read every book in the library. They have shipped nothing. They will not push back unless you ask. They will not check their work unless you tell them how. They will write 1,800 confident words on any topic, and they cannot tell when they are wrong.

That is your Claude. It is not less than this and it is not more. Once you hold this picture, every other rule in this course follows.

blocks.md:
Anthropic ships three surfaces in 2026: **Claude.ai** (web chat, with Projects and Artifacts), **Claude Code** (CLI in your terminal with file and shell access), and the **Anthropic API** (raw access for your own software). Three models live on each: **Opus 4.7** with the 1M-token context window for hard reasoning, **Sonnet 4.6** as the best-cost workhorse, and **Haiku 4.5** for cheap, fast, repetitive jobs.

The map is not just product trivia. It is the first decision you make every time you open Claude. Wrong surface plus wrong model is a 10x cost mistake or a 10x quality mistake. The map collapses to one rule: **Claude.ai for thinking with you, Claude Code for changing files for you, API for doing the same thing 1,000 times for you**. Once you can place a task on this map in three seconds, you save yourself half the prompts you would have written.

blocks.prompt: You need to rename a function across 23 files in a Next.js repo. Which surface fits?

choices.label: Claude.ai with the files pasted in
choices.explain: Pasting 23 files is wasteful and Claude.ai cannot write back to your filesystem.

choices.label: Claude Code
choices.explain: Multi-file edits with grep + apply-patch tools are the bread and butter of Claude Code.

choices.label: Anthropic API with a custom script
choices.explain: Possible, but you are reinventing what Claude Code already does.

choices.label: Skip Claude — sed will do it
choices.explain: Sed will rename text but break call-sites with type signatures or string literals. The point of Claude Code is the verification.

hi-IN.title: Manager ka famous dialogue
hi-IN.md: Manager ne meeting mein bola, *'arre yaar, Claude se draft karwao na'*. Junior ne 12 minute mein bana diya. Manager ne signing apne se kara, **without reading**. Client meeting mein client bola *'aapne MCA Section 23A ka reference diya, Companies Act mein toh Section 23B hai'*. Pure team ka mood off. Lesson? Don't ask Claude what you don't already know enough to verify. Show it your draft, let it find holes. Reverse the direction.

en.title: The manager who didn't read
en.md: Manager asked Claude to 'draft something quick'. Sent it without reading. Client noticed the regulation citation pointed to a section that does not exist. The fix is not to use Claude less; it is to ask better. Don't ask Claude what you can't verify. Show Claude your draft and let it find holes.

blocks.md:
There are two ways to start a Claude conversation. The bad one: *'write me a marketing plan for a Bengaluru fintech going into Tier 2 cities'*. The good one: *'here is our current Tier 1 marketing plan, here is what we know about Indore and Coimbatore from our last user research, here is what our CFO will not approve, find the three weakest assumptions in the obvious extension to Tier 2'*.

The first prompt asks Claude to invent. Claude is a confident inventor and you have no way to verify. The second prompt asks Claude to **critique a draft** that you can already evaluate. Now the failure mode flips: instead of you trying to spot fabrications in 1,800 words, Claude is trying to find holes in a 400-word draft you wrote. That is a structurally easier review.

Name this move: **don't ask, show**. Ninety percent of the value of Claude in a knowledge job comes from showing it work and asking for critique, not asking it for first drafts.

intro: Right. I see this every week. Founders open Claude, type the first thing that comes to mind, and act surprised when the answer is generic.
Sort each scenario into ASK or SHOW or NOT-CLAUDE. The third bucket exists because some things Claude should not be doing at all.

scenarios.situation: You wrote a one-pager pitching a new pricing tier. You want to know if it is convincing.
scenarios.explain: Classic SHOW. You wrote it, you can evaluate the critique, the failure mode is small.

scenarios.situation: You need a list of 30 fintech competitors in India with current revenue.
scenarios.explain: Without a real data tool, Claude will fabricate revenues with three-digit precision. Use Tracxn, Crunchbase or AlphaSense, not Claude.

scenarios.situation: You have never written a SOC 2 readiness checklist and want a starting structure.
scenarios.explain: Legitimate ASK. You will then verify with your auditor. Accept that you are signing up for a review pass.

scenarios.situation: Your CTO sent a 600-line PR. You want a second opinion before approving.
scenarios.explain: SHOW with the diff attached. Ask Claude to find the three riskiest changes, then you decide.

scenarios.situation: You want today's USD-INR rate to put in a slide.
scenarios.explain: Use a price API or Google. Claude without web search will give you yesterday's number and call it today.

scenarios.situation: You have a draft email rejecting a candidate. You want it to be kinder without being false.
scenarios.explain: SHOW. Your draft, Claude tightens. The judgement of 'kind' stays yours.

blocks.title: The classic trap: confidence without grounding
blocks.md: When Claude has no source, it does not say 'I don't know'. It pattern-matches to plausible-sounding text. This is the **fabrication failure**, and it is the single largest risk in your first month using Claude. Defenses: turn on web search for current facts, attach source files for domain claims, use Projects to pin a knowledge base, and assume any specific number, citation or proper name in Claude output is wrong until you check.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka cross-examination
hi-IN.md: Bhai, Mummy ka rule yaad hai? *'Khud likh ke dikha, fir bataungi kya theek nahi hai.'* Same with Claude. Apna draft do, fir critique maango. Khali question puchhne se mummy bhi vague answer deti thi: *'soch ke bata.'* Claude bhi same. Don't ask, show — yeh life-skill hai, sirf AI ki nahi.

en.title: The mom move
en.md: Mom never reviewed an empty page. She would say 'show me what you have, then I'll tell you what's wrong'. Claude responds the same way. Empty asks get vague answers; concrete drafts get sharp critique. Don't ask, show is older than AI.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Live Stock Price That Wasn't
blocks.source: Anonymous board observer at NimbusPay, a Mumbai-based series-A payments startup
blocks.story:
On February 11, 2026, NimbusPay's CTO walked into a board meeting with a slide titled *"Claude Can Do Anything."* He had been demoing Opus 4.7 with the 1M-context window for three weeks and had genuinely convinced himself this was true. The board, two of whom run public-market funds, were the wrong audience for unfounded enthusiasm.

The demo: he opened Claude.ai, typed *"What is the current NSE price of HDFC Bank?"*, and waited for the magic. Claude, with no web tool enabled, helpfully produced a confident answer: **₹1,712.40 as of today**. The board member from the public-market fund pulled up his Bloomberg terminal. Actual price, that minute: **₹1,684.55**.

Silence. Then the slow, patient question: *"Was that a guess?"* The CTO checked. No web search tool. No MCP connector. Just a model hallucinating a plausible number from training data that was 14 months old.

The board didn't kill the AI program. They did demand a written **capability map** — what Claude can do alone vs. with tools vs. not at all — within two weeks. The CTO spent a weekend writing it. He now opens every demo with the line *"Here's what it can't do."*
blocks.takeaway: Claude without tools is a brilliant intern with no internet, no calculator, and a confident voice. Map the capability surface before you map the demo.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Week 1 — The CTO's AI Feature Wishlist
blocks.setup:
It's **week 1 of Q1 2026**. You are **Karthik, dev at Velora**, a Bengaluru fintech with ~80 engineers. The CTO just forwarded you a Slack message: *"Board wants an AI feature shipped by end of Q1. Here are five ideas they brainstormed. Pick what we ship and what we politely refuse — by Friday."*

The list: **(1)** real-time market-news summarizer, **(2)** internal-policy Q&A bot, **(3)** AI customer-service agent that auto-issues refunds, **(4)** dev-productivity copilot for the engineering team, **(5)** auto-generated quarterly investor letter.

You have one Friday afternoon, one rollout budget, and a board that just learned the word *hallucination*.

coach.name: VP-of-AI Vidya
coach.role: Joined Velora last quarter from a unicorn that shipped 11 AI features and killed 9

stages.prompt: Vidya pulls up a chair. *"Before you pick, what's the **one filter** you apply to every idea?"*

options.label: "Can Claude do it without tools, today, in one shot?"
options.explain: **Right filter.** This separates the *demoable* from the *operationally risky*. If it needs live data, multi-step tool use, or zero-error output, you're not shipping in Q1 — you're shipping a liability.

options.label: "Which one will impress the board the most?"
options.explain: Vidya winces. Board-impressing AI is how you end up demoing live stock prices that are 14 months stale. Optimize for *reliable*, not *impressive*.

options.label: "Which one has the biggest revenue lift?"
options.explain: Revenue is a tiebreaker, not a filter. The auto-refund agent has the biggest revenue impact and the biggest blast radius — picking by revenue first lands you in regulatory review.

options.label: "Which one already has a Claude-shaped solution in the docs?"
options.explain: **Solid.** Anthropic's published patterns (projects, MCP, subagents) are a strong signal of what's *production-ready* vs. what's *research-grade*. Match the idea to a known surface.

stages.prompt: Apply the filter. **Which two ship in Q1?**

options.label: Internal-policy Q&A bot + dev-productivity copilot.
options.explain: **Yes.** Both are bounded, internal, and forgiving. Policy Q&A becomes a Claude Project with the policy PDFs attached. Copilot becomes Claude Code with a `CLAUDE.md` kernel. If they hallucinate, the blast radius is one engineer rolling their eyes — not a refund issued in error.

options.label: Real-time market-news summarizer + auto-refund agent.
options.explain: Both fail the filter on day one. Market summarizer needs live data Claude doesn't have. Auto-refund touches money and customers — exactly where hallucination becomes a regulatory event. Hard pass.

options.label: Auto-generated investor letter + market-news summarizer.
options.explain: An AI-drafted investor letter sounds clever until the first sentence contains a fabricated figure and an LP forwards it to SEBI. Investor comms is the *last* thing you automate, not the first.

options.label: Dev-productivity copilot + AI customer-service agent (read-only, no refunds).
options.explain: **Defensible.** You stripped the dangerous verb (*auto-issues refunds*) and kept the safe one (*answers questions, escalates*). This is the right way to descope: keep the surface, remove the irreversible action.

stages.prompt: The CTO replies: *"Cool, but the board specifically asked for the auto-refund agent. Push back or comply?"*

options.label: Comply. The board signs the cheques.
options.explain: The board also fires the CTO when an AI agent issues ₹40 lakh in incorrect refunds in one weekend. Compliance without challenge is how senior engineers earn the title 'former senior engineer.'

options.label: Push back with a written one-pager: capability gap, blast radius, and a phased alternative (AI drafts refund, human approves).
options.explain: **This is the move.** You didn't say no — you said *not yet, and here's the version that ships safely*. Human-in-the-loop on the irreversible step is the standard pattern. Vidya is already redlining the doc.

options.label: Run a 50-customer pilot first, see what breaks.
options.explain: **Also good.** A bounded pilot with manual reconciliation gives you real failure data instead of a theoretical argument. Just make sure 'see what breaks' has a tripwire — auto-pause at 3 errors, not 300.

options.label: Build it but quietly route every refund through a human approval queue without telling the board.
options.explain: Now you have a hidden human bottleneck the board thinks is automated. When latency spikes, the CTO has to explain why the 'AI agent' is actually three people in a Notion table. Trust loss is permanent.

stages.prompt: Final week-1 deliverable: a **one-page capability map** for the company. What's on it?

options.label: Three columns: *Claude alone* / *Claude + tools (MCP, web)* / *Don't use Claude*. With one Velora example per cell.
options.explain: **Exactly the artifact.** This is the document the CTO can hand to any PM, any engineer, any board member, and they know what's possible *today*. Vidya pins it in #engineering.

options.label: A long list of 'best practices' copied from Anthropic's docs.
options.explain: Best-practices docs are read by no one. A one-page decision aid with Velora-specific examples is read by everyone. Generic content has no half-life.

options.label: Just a Slack message saying 'use Claude for X, not Y'.
options.explain: The Slack message disappears in 48 hours and nobody onboarded after that ever sees it. Decisions need durable artifacts, not ephemeral ones.

options.label: The three columns *plus* a 'Reviewed: 2026-05-07' date and an owner so it gets refreshed quarterly.
options.explain: **Top tier.** Capability maps go stale fast — Sonnet 4.6 to Opus 4.7 was a real boundary shift. Dating the doc and assigning an owner is the difference between a living artifact and a museum piece.

outcomes.perfect: Week 1 done right. You filtered with capability, not vibes. Picked two safe-to-ship ideas, descoped the dangerous one to human-in-the-loop, and left behind a one-page artifact that survives your laptop dying. **Vidya forwards your map to the CTO unedited.**
outcomes.good: You got the big calls right but made one or two scope-creep mistakes. Re-read the lesson on *what Claude can't do without tools* — that filter is the entire job in week 1.
outcomes.learn: You shipped what the board asked for, not what was safe to ship. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **capability gaps** and **blast-radius scoping**. Velora gets one shot at first impressions; make week 1 boring on purpose.

blocks.md: Most engineers meet Claude Code expecting fancy autocomplete. They open the terminal, type *'add a login button'*, watch it run for forty minutes, and either get something brilliant or something that touched 14 files including the build config. Both outcomes feel like luck because both **are** luck. Claude Code rewards a specific working style: plan first, then execute, with a kernel file that remembers your standards. Without that, you are running a fast junior on caffeine in your filesystem at 2am. With it, Claude Code shipping work is the most leveraged hour of your day.

en.md: A Pune SaaS asked Claude Code to migrate from Express to Fastify in one shot. 84 files later, the build was broken and half the routes were 500-ing. They git reset, wrote a CLAUDE.md kernel, ran /plan first, then /implement. The second pass took 11 days with zero rollback. Same model, same task, completely different outcome.

blocks.md:
Every non-trivial task should start with a planning subagent that reads code and writes a plan, **without modifying anything**. The built-in `Plan` subagent does exactly this. It investigates the codebase, asks clarifying questions, and produces `docs/PLAN.md` in a canonical format: goal, files touched, approach, risks, rollback. Then a separate run executes the plan.

Why split? Three reasons. First, **planning catches contradictions** before they become 14 broken files. Second, **the plan is reviewable in two minutes** while the diff is reviewable in two hours. Third, **a paused plan is cheap to throw away**; a half-done execution is expensive. Run `/plan` for anything that touches 3+ files, anything in auth or payments or migrations, and anything where you are not 100 percent sure of the right approach. Run it even when you are sure; you will be surprised how often you were wrong.

en.title: Production-ready auth in one prompt
en.md: An intern asked Claude Code for production-ready auth in one prompt. It installed 6 packages, invented 11 environment variables, and created 23 files. The senior spent 30 minutes understanding it, then deleted everything. The fix is not 'never use Claude Code'; it is to write CLAUDE.md rules that say 'auth changes need /plan' and 'no new env vars without docs entry'. Rules are cheaper than reviews.

blocks.md:
CLAUDE.md is a markdown file at the root of your repo that Claude Code reads at the start of every session. It is your **kernel** in the Linux sense: a small, durable, always-loaded set of rules that constrain everything else. A good kernel has six things: stack nouns, key commands, hard rules (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), slash commands, load-on-demand pointers to deeper docs, and known issues.

What does this buy you? **Reproducibility**. Two different engineers running Claude Code on your repo get the same standards. **Speed**. Common protocols collapse to one slash command. **Safety**. The hard-rules section blocks the things that would otherwise need a code review to catch. Claude Code without CLAUDE.md is just expensive autocomplete. Claude Code with a 200-line kernel is a teammate who has read your style guide, your testing strategy, and the postmortems.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the unbounded subagent
blocks.md: Subagents are powerful: `general-purpose` for multi-step research, `Plan` for read-only planning, `bug-hunter` for finding the root cause of a failure, `pr-reviewer` for reading a diff, `Explore` for codebase orientation. The trap: launching a subagent without a bounded brief and a hard stop. *'Investigate why the build is slow'* is unbounded; *'investigate why the build is slow, focus on the webpack config and the test pipeline, return a 5-bullet diagnosis'* is bounded. Unbounded subagents drift, cost more, and produce essays you have to read. Always give them a brief and a deliverable.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Bugfix That Refactored the Auth Module
blocks.source: Engineering manager at Pratham Logistics, a Gurugram-based series-B B2B logistics platform
blocks.story:
In November 2025, Pratham's platform team adopted Claude Code CLI across 22 engineers. They skipped the `CLAUDE.md` step. *"We'll add it later — let's just start shipping,"* one staff engineer said in the kickoff. They started shipping. Things moved fast for about nine days.

On the tenth day, a junior engineer asked Claude Code to fix a one-line null-check bug in the booking-confirmation flow. Forty-seven minutes later, Claude had refactored the entire **authentication module** because — in the absence of any project context — it decided the *real* problem was that the codebase used callback-style auth handlers and "modern best practice" was async/await. The PR was 134 files. The null-check was, in fact, fixed. So was the auth module. So was three weeks of sprint capacity.

The team paused, wrote a 600-line `CLAUDE.md` over two days, and re-ran the experiment. Same junior. Same bug. **Six minutes**. Two-line PR. Auth module untouched. Over the next quarter, **PR-to-merge time dropped 40%** and the team killed three of the four "Claude is making things weird" Slack threads.

The missing kernel was the entire problem. Nobody at Pratham starts a Claude Code session without one anymore.
blocks.takeaway: Claude Code without a `CLAUDE.md` is a brilliant contractor who has never seen your codebase and assumes every refactor is welcome. The kernel is the single highest-leverage file in your repo.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Week 4 — Karthik's First Claude Code Task
blocks.setup:
**Week 4 of Q1 2026.** The capability map shipped. The CTO greenlit the dev-productivity copilot rollout. **Velora's 80 engineers** start onboarding to Claude Code Monday. You — Karthik — get to be patient zero.

Your first real task: a flaky integration test in `payments-service` (Velora's mid-size Node service, ~40k lines, 4 active contributors). Test fails 1 in 8 runs. Three engineers have looked at it. You have Claude Code installed, an open terminal, and exactly **zero** project files configured.

coach.name: Anthropic-Veteran Anuj
coach.role: Spent 18 months at a Claude-Code-first startup before joining Velora as principal engineer

stages.prompt: Anuj sits down beside you. *"Before you type a single prompt, what's your **first move** in the repo?"*

options.label: `claude` and start typing: *"There's a flaky test in payments-service, fix it."*
options.explain: No kernel, no context, no scope. Claude will either spelunk the entire repo guessing what *flaky* means here, or — worse — refactor the test framework because it decides Mocha is 'legacy.' This is exactly how Pratham lost three weeks.

options.label: Write a `CLAUDE.md` at repo root: stack, key commands (test, lint, typecheck), conventions, and 'never touch' files.
options.explain: **Yes.** The kernel is the contract. Even a 200-line `CLAUDE.md` with stack nouns and a 'don't touch the migrations directory' line will save you four hours of cleanup. Anuj nods.

options.label: Skip the kernel for now — just paste the failing test output into Claude.ai instead.
options.explain: Now you're using a chat interface to debug a codebase, with no agent loop, no file access, and no ability to actually run the test. You traded one bad pattern for a worse one.

options.label: Write `CLAUDE.md` *and* a `docs/PLAN.md` since this touches a service three other engineers contribute to.
options.explain: **Top-tier.** Plan-before-act for any change in shared territory. Even a 10-line plan ('hypothesis: race condition in webhook handler; check X, Y, Z; one change at a time') keeps Claude on rails.

stages.prompt: You write the kernel. **What goes in it that prevents the Pratham incident?**

options.label: Stack list, `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, that's it.
options.explain: Half a kernel. Stack and commands are necessary but not sufficient — without scope rules, Claude still feels free to refactor anything it touches.

options.label: Add a **Hard Rules** section: 'No refactors outside the file you're editing without explicit approval. No new dependencies without `/plan`. Touch only the failing test and its direct call graph.'
options.explain: **This is the load-bearing section.** Hard rules with MUST/SHOULD/MAY semantics give Claude a clear veto framework. The Pratham auth-refactor would have been blocked by a single MUST line.

options.label: Add a 'Current Focus' section: 'Debugging flaky test in `payments-service/webhooks.spec.ts`. Hypothesis: timer-related race.'
options.explain: **Excellent.** Current Focus tells Claude what session-level state to optimize for. It also tells *future Karthik* what week-4 Karthik was doing when he got pulled into a meeting.

options.label: Just paste in Anthropic's example `CLAUDE.md` from the docs.
options.explain: Generic kernels are worse than no kernel — they give Claude false confidence about a codebase that doesn't match the template. You need *Velora-specific* nouns, paths, and conventions.

stages.prompt: Kernel is in. You start the session. Claude proposes a fix that touches 3 files, including one in `auth-service`. **What now?**

options.label: Approve. Claude is usually right; let it ship.
options.explain: *Auth-service* is outside the scope you set. The fact that Claude wants to go there is a *signal*, not a green light. Approving silently is how scope rules become decorative.

options.label: Stop, ask Claude to *explain* why it needs to touch `auth-service`, then decide.
options.explain: **Right move.** If the explanation is 'the webhook handler reads the auth token through this helper,' that's legitimate — narrow it to a one-line read. If the explanation is 'I noticed the auth code could be cleaner,' that's the Pratham move. Reject.

options.label: Reject the fix entirely and ask for one that only touches `payments-service`.
options.explain: **Defensible.** Forcing scope is a valid coaching signal. You may get a less elegant fix, but you'll get one inside your blast radius — and you'll learn whether Claude can solve the problem within the constraint.

options.label: Approve, then in the same session ask Claude to *also* refactor `auth-service` to be 'more consistent.'
options.explain: Anuj physically removes your hand from the keyboard. You just turned a one-test bugfix into a multi-service refactor with no plan, no review, and no safety net. This is the Pratham incident in real-time.

stages.prompt: Fix lands. Tests green. **Last step before you mark this as 'rollout-ready' for the other 79 engineers?**

options.label: Slack the team: 'Claude Code works, here's the install link.'
options.explain: Now 79 engineers install Claude Code, write zero kernels, and Pratham happens to Velora over a single weekend. The CLI is 5% of the rollout; the workflow is 95%.

options.label: Promote the `CLAUDE.md` you wrote to a repo template + write a 1-page rollout doc: kernel-first, plan-before-act, scope rules.
options.explain: **Exactly right.** Codify the workflow that worked. The repo template makes the right thing the easy thing — every new service gets a kernel by default, not by hope.

options.label: Run the same experiment on two more services, prove the 40% PR-to-merge improvement, *then* roll out.
options.explain: **Top-tier.** Three datapoints beats one. You have a real number to show the CTO and a real artifact (the kernels) to ship with. Anuj is taking notes.

options.label: Tell Anuj it worked and move on to the next ticket.
options.explain: Working once is a coincidence. Working three times with documentation is a rollout. You skipped the part where individual success becomes organizational capability.

outcomes.perfect: You wrote the kernel, scoped the work, caught the scope creep, and turned a personal win into a team artifact. **Anuj is already drafting the all-hands slide that uses your kernel as the example.** Velora's rollout starts on rails.
outcomes.good: You avoided the worst mistakes but missed a step or two on codifying the workflow. Re-read the lesson on **kernel-first sessions** — the difference between 'I made it work' and 'the team makes it work' is in the artifacts you leave behind.
outcomes.learn: You shipped a fix and a future Pratham incident in the same week. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **CLAUDE.md as a contract** and **plan-before-act in shared code**. Velora has 80 engineers about to copy your habits; make sure the habits are worth copying.

points: Claude Code without CLAUDE.md is expensive autocomplete; with a kernel it is a teammate.
Always /plan before /implement for anything 3+ files, auth, payments, or migrations.
The plan is reviewable in 2 minutes; the diff is reviewable in 2 hours. Cheaper to be wrong on the plan.
Subagents need bounded briefs and a deliverable; unbounded subagents drift.
Hooks enforce the rules you would otherwise have to enforce in code review.

lessons.title: Claude as a Coworker — Slack, Email, Meetings
lessons.subtitle: A draft engine, not the sender

blocks.md: Cowork is the use case where Claude looks easy and is actually the most dangerous. Unlike code, where a broken build screams at you, a Claude-drafted Slack message that subtly misrepresents what your CFO said only fails 48 hours later when the CFO sees it in a thread. The error is silent and reputational. The whole game in this lesson is to use Claude aggressively for **drafts** while building unbreakable discipline around **review and send**. The teams that get this right ship 30 percent more communication with the same headcount; the teams that get it wrong end up with a 'we don't trust AI' policy that throws out the baby.

en.title: The AI prefix that survived
en.md: A junior PM at a fintech sent a DM to the CEO that opened with 'As an AI language model, I would like to thank you for the opportunity'. The CEO screenshotted it. The PM kept their job; their reputation took six months to come back. The fix is one read-through. Five seconds.

blocks.md:
Make it a rule, not a vibe. **No message generated by Claude leaves your account without a full read-through and at least one substantive edit**. Two parts; both are non-negotiable.

Full read-through catches the obvious AI tells: the *'as an AI language model'* opener, the seven-bullet symmetry, the em-dash addiction, the *'in conclusion'* paragraph nobody asked for. Substantive edit forces you to claim the message — change a sentence, cut a paragraph, add a name, reorder a point. Without an edit you are publishing under your name something you did not really write. The reader smells it. The trust cost compounds.

For recurring formats — weekly updates, standup posts, status reports — build a personal Project on Claude.ai with three to five of your own previous good examples pinned. Now Claude's drafts arrive pre-shaped to your voice, and the review burden drops to seconds.

en.title: The smell of generic prose
en.md: If your standup posts say 'made significant progress on yesterday's tasks, blockers minimal' five days in a row, the team can smell Claude. Real updates have specifics: file numbers, names, line counts, blockers by name. Generic prose is the AI tell; specificity is the proof of work.

blocks.md:
Ninety percent of professional writing is *'I have the points; I need them in flowing prose for an audience'*. Status updates, board notes, performance reviews, postmortems, RFP responses, even most LinkedIn posts. The leverage move is to **write the bullets yourself in 90 seconds**, then hand them to Claude with three pieces of context: who is reading, what tone fits, and what house-style examples to match.

This is the bullet-to-paragraph expander. It works because the bullets carry your judgement (what to include, what to leave out, what to emphasise) and Claude carries the prose (transitions, flow, tone calibration). The opposite mistake is asking Claude for a *first-pass status update* with no bullets. Then Claude invents what to say, you discover it half-wrong, and you spend more time editing than you would have spent writing it from scratch.

For a Slack post: 3 bullets in. For a board update: 8 bullets in. For a postmortem: a structured bullet list with timeline, root cause, fix. For a customer email: bullets plus the original message. The expander is the highest-frequency Claude use in your week; make it muscle memory.

intro: Most of these scenarios show up in your first month using Claude at work. Sort each into the right bucket.
Be honest. Some of these are tempting because they save time but cost trust.

scenarios.situation: You bullet your weekly update, paste it in your personal Project, get a draft in your voice, edit two sentences, send.
scenarios.explain: Textbook bullet-to-paragraph expander with style anchored to past examples.

scenarios.situation: You ask Claude to write a 'difficult feedback' message to a teammate without telling Claude any context about the relationship.
scenarios.explain: Could be good if you provide context: the history, what you've already said, what specifically went wrong. Without that, generic and unsafe.

scenarios.situation: You set up a Slack bot that auto-replies to customer messages with Claude-generated text.
scenarios.explain: Autonomous send violates the no-send-without-review rule. Even one wrong reply on a real complaint is a reputation event.

scenarios.situation: Recording a meeting, Claude transcribes, you ask Claude to summarise actions, you edit and post in Slack.
scenarios.explain: Summary plus your edit is a clean loop. Just make sure participants know you are recording (legal in India with consent).

scenarios.situation: Your CEO sends you a one-line ask. You forward it to Claude with 'reply for me'. Claude invents commitments you can't keep.
scenarios.explain: Bullet first, expand second. The fix is process, not avoiding Claude.

scenarios.situation: You ghostwrite a LinkedIn post entirely with Claude, edit nothing, post under your name.
scenarios.explain: Reputation play. Readers can tell. The personal-brand cost is bigger than the time saved.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the asymmetry of small wins and big losses
blocks.md: Cowork is a domain where 95 percent of Claude-drafted messages are fine and 5 percent are catastrophic — wrong tone to a board member, fabricated commitment to a customer, leaked confidential context, AI-prefix in a CEO DM. Treating each message individually leads to *'it's been fine so far'* complacency. The right framing: **the cost of one bad message is asymmetric**. One wrong message to a regulator can cost ₹2 crore. One wrong message to a candidate can lose them. One wrong message to your CEO can make you the punchline for a quarter. The review gate exists for the 5 percent.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Slack Auto-Send That Cited a Fake Metric
blocks.source: Director of Engineering at Khaata Cloud, a Pune-based series-A SaaS startup
blocks.story:
On December 3, 2025, Khaata's growth lead set up a Claude-Slack MCP integration with a single autonomous workflow: *"Every Monday at 9am, post a one-paragraph weekly metrics summary to #all-hands."* He hooked it to a metrics dashboard, gave it the channel write-permission, and went on holiday. He did not put a human in the loop.

The first three Mondays were fine. On December 22 — the fourth Monday — the metrics API timed out. Claude, helpfully, did not fail loudly. It produced a summary anyway, drawing on the *previous week's cached numbers* and a vague memory of the company's general trajectory. The post claimed **"Weekly active users grew 18% week-on-week to 47,000."**

Real number, that morning: **a 4% decline to 31,200**. Off by 51% on the trend, off by 16,000 on the absolute. The post stayed up for 4 hours before the head of data noticed. It had been **screenshotted by 11 employees**, two of whom forwarded it to LPs as part of casual investor updates. The retraction post got 1/8th the views.

Internal post-mortem found no malice and no bug — the system worked as designed. The design was the bug. **It took the team 4 weeks to rebuild trust** in any AI-generated number going into Slack. The integration is now draft-only with a named human approver per channel.
blocks.takeaway: Auto-send is the most expensive feature you can enable in any cowork integration. The right default is *draft + notify*, not *send*.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Week 8 — The First AI-Drafted Email to the CFO
blocks.setup:
**Week 8 of Q1 2026.** Velora's Claude Code rollout is humming. The cowork rollout starts this week — Claude in Slack (via MCP), Claude in Gmail (via the Workspace connector), Claude in meeting notes. You — Karthik — get tapped to draft Velora's *first* AI-assisted email **to the CFO** explaining a Q1 engineering budget overrun (₹14 lakh over plan, mostly AWS).

The CFO, **Meera**, is famously skeptical of AI. She has read three of those *"ChatGPT made up case law"* news stories and quotes them at meetings. You have one shot to make her trust this workflow — or to set the cowork rollout back six months.

coach.name: VP-of-AI Vidya
coach.role: Has watched four companies fumble exactly this email

stages.prompt: Vidya plants herself at your desk. *"Step one. What's the **single rule** for this email?"*

options.label: "Claude drafts. I read every line. I send. No auto-send, ever, for this surface."
options.explain: **The right rule, full stop.** *Draft → human review → human send.* This is the rule that survives the Khaata incident and 90% of all other AI cowork failures. Vidya audibly exhales.

options.label: "Use Claude for the first draft, then have Claude review its own draft."
options.explain: Self-review is theater. Claude marking its own homework will catch typos and miss the fabricated number. The reviewer must be a human who knows the actual ₹14 lakh story.

options.label: "Set up the Gmail MCP to send automatically once Claude is 'confident.'"
options.explain: Confidence is not calibration. Claude was confident at Khaata too. Auto-send to a CFO is the Slack incident with longer paper trail and senior recipients.

options.label: "Draft, review, *and* attach the source numbers as a separate doc so Meera can verify."
options.explain: **Top-tier.** Verifiable claims build trust faster than confident prose. Meera will check the doc once, find the numbers match, and trust the next draft 30% more.

stages.prompt: You open Claude.ai, start a new project, and feed it context. **What goes in?**

options.label: Just the budget overrun number and 'write a one-paragraph email to the CFO.'
options.explain: Claude will produce a beautifully-written paragraph that hallucinates the *cause*, the *plan*, and possibly Meera's preferred salutation. Garbage in, fluent garbage out.

options.label: The original Q1 budget plan, the actual AWS bills broken down by service, the engineering team's note on what drove the overrun, and Meera's last 3 emails (to match her tone).
options.explain: **Right level of context.** Now Claude has the real story to summarize and the real voice to mimic. The draft will be 80% there, and your edits will be substantive (numbers, framing) not cosmetic (tone).

options.label: Everything from the Velora finance Notion + every CFO-related Slack channel, just in case.
options.explain: Now you've leaked half the company's financial context into a chat session and given Claude so much noise it'll cherry-pick whichever facts produce the most flattering story. Less is more.

options.label: The budget plan, the AWS breakdown, the engineering note — *and* a one-line constraint: 'Do not invent root causes; if uncertain, say so.'
options.explain: **Excellent.** The instruction is the load-bearing line. It tells Claude that *uncertainty is a valid output*. Without it, you get false confidence; with it, you get '...the remaining ₹2 lakh is unaccounted for and we are investigating.'

stages.prompt: Draft is back. It's good. **One sentence catches your eye:** *"This overrun was driven primarily by a 34% spike in S3 egress related to the new analytics pipeline."* You don't actually know if 34% is right. **What do you do?**

options.label: Send it. The number sounds plausible and the email is otherwise great.
options.explain: This is the Khaata move in a 1:1 channel. *Plausible* is not *true*. Meera will check the AWS console in 90 seconds and find the real number is 12%. Trust gone, possibly permanently.

options.label: Open the AWS console, verify the number, edit if wrong.
options.explain: **This is the job.** Every load-bearing number gets verified before it leaves your outbox. The friction is the point — it forces a human between the model and the recipient.

options.label: Ask Claude: 'Are you sure about 34%?'
options.explain: Claude will confidently double down or confidently retract — neither is verification. The model has no way to check the actual S3 bill. Only you do.

options.label: Replace the specific number with 'a significant spike' and move on.
options.explain: **Acceptable.** Removing the unverified specific is safer than guessing. The email loses some sharpness but gains zero risk of being wrong. Meera will respect the precision-where-precise approach.

stages.prompt: You hit send. Email lands well. Meera replies *"thanks for the clear breakdown."* **Now what?**

options.label: Slack the team: 'Claude wrote that CFO email — see, it works!'
options.explain: You just told 80 engineers that AI-drafted CFO emails are fine. Some of them will skip the *human review* step entirely. You have repeated Khaata's onboarding error.

options.label: Write a short internal post: 'I used Claude to draft, I verified every number, I sent. Here's the workflow — copy *this*, not the shortcut.'
options.explain: **Exactly the right framing.** Codify the *workflow*, not the *outcome*. The post becomes the template; the template becomes the norm. Vidya pins it.

options.label: Set up a Slack reaction-based 'AI-drafted, human-sent' tag so anyone using this pattern marks their messages.
options.explain: **Light-touch governance.** The tag is voluntary, transparent, and creates a soft norm without bureaucracy. Six months later you can audit which channels use it and where the workflow needs reinforcement.

options.label: Quietly enable Gmail auto-send for low-stakes threads like 'meeting reschedules.'
options.explain: There is no such thing as 'low-stakes' auto-send. The first auto-sent meeting reschedule that mis-states the time wastes 8 people's morning. Stay in draft mode until you have *measured* false-positive rates.

outcomes.perfect: You drafted, verified, sent, *and* taught the team. Meera trusts the workflow, Vidya is taking notes for next quarter's ops review, and Velora's cowork rollout has a real artifact to copy. **The Khaata incident is now a story you can tell, not one you'll relive.**
outcomes.good: You handled your own email well but left the team rollout slightly under-codified. Re-read the lesson on **draft → review → send** as a *cultural norm*, not a personal habit — the second one doesn't scale to 80 engineers.
outcomes.learn: You either auto-sent a number you couldn't verify, or you sent a great email and let the team draw the wrong lesson. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **why auto-send is the highest-cost cowork feature**. Trust takes 4 weeks to rebuild and 4 minutes to lose.

No-send-without-review: full read-through plus at least one substantive edit, every time.
The bullet-to-paragraph expander is the highest-frequency cowork move; you hold judgement, Claude holds prose.
Pin 3-5 of your own past examples in a Project so Claude drafts arrive in your voice.
The cost of one bad message is asymmetric; the review gate exists for the 5 percent that matter.

lessons.title: Claude Design: Mockups, Copy, Critique
lessons.subtitle: A junior designer who has read every book and shipped nothing

audioChapters.label: Why design with Claude is tricky

blocks.md: Designers come to Claude with two opposite expectations and both are wrong. The first expectation: *Claude will generate beautiful mockups for me*. It will not — Claude does not produce images, it produces text descriptions of images, and even those are generic unless aggressively constrained. The second expectation: *Claude knows nothing about design, so why bother*. Also wrong — Claude has read every design book, every Nielsen Norman article, every IDEO case study. It is the most well-read junior designer you could hire. The right framing sits in between: Claude is a junior designer who has read everything and designed nothing. You bring the taste; Claude brings the vocabulary, the critique, and the grunt work.

blocks.md: Picture the most well-read junior designer in the country. They can quote Krug on usability, Wroblewski on forms, Norman on signifiers, Saffer on micro-interactions. blocks.md:
The single highest-leverage Claude design move is this: **show your mockup to Claude with a named user, a named goal, and a named primary action; ask Claude to identify the three weakest decisions before suggesting fixes**. Notice everything that constrains the answer. The user is named (*'a 38-year-old shop-owner in Surat ordering wholesale supplies on her phone, one-handed, in a noisy market'*). The goal is named (*'place a repeat order in under 90 seconds'*). The primary action is named (*'tap reorder, confirm address, pay'*). Now Claude cannot drift into generic SaaS advice; it has to evaluate the screen against a real scenario.

The opposite move — *'design me a checkout screen for a B2B marketplace'* — is what every founder tries first. Claude returns a generic best-practice template that ignores everything you already considered. You spend more time explaining why the suggestion does not fit than you would have spent designing from scratch. Critique-not-generate flips the cost: instead of you reviewing 800 words of Claude proposal, Claude reviews your 1 mockup against your 3 constraints. That is a 10x easier loop.

hi-IN.title: Aunty test
hi-IN.md: Bhai, design ka pehla test toh hamesha *'aunty test'*. Tumhari mummy aur unki teen friends. Bina explanation ke screenshot dikhao. Agar woh primary action 4 second mein point kar sakti hain, design clean hai. Claude woh test simulate kar sakta hai — *'pretend you're a 55-year-old Aunty, never used this app, what do you tap first'*. Sometimes Claude bolega *'I'd tap the giant blue button'* — galat answer, kyunki actual aunty would tap the photo first because pattern recognition. Use Claude as a baseline; Aunty as the truth.

en.title: The aunty test
en.md: First test of any design is the aunty test: a 55-year-old who has never seen the app, looking at a screenshot. Can she point to the primary action in 4 seconds? Claude can simulate that test (it has read the research) but Claude is a model of an aunty, not the actual one. Use Claude as a fast baseline. Use a real aunty as the truth.

blocks.md:
Designs do not get good in one round. They get good in **3-5 rounds where each round tightens one specific constraint**. Round one is critique against the user goal. Round two is copy: every word on the screen, in your voice, under a length cap. Round three is edge cases: empty state, error state, slow network. Round four is accessibility: contrast, tap targets, keyboard nav. Round five is the trade-off summary: what you intentionally sacrificed and why.

Claude is the perfect partner for this loop because each round is small, bounded, and reviewable in five minutes. The temptation is to ask Claude for *'all of this in one round'*. Don't. The output is mush, the review is exhausting, and you cannot tell which round of critique you accepted vs rejected. **One constraint per round** keeps the loop crisp.

For copy specifically, the iterative-tightening loop has its own rhythm. Paste the screen text. Ask Claude to *'cut by 30 percent without losing meaning'*. Then *'rewrite for the user voice — they're a busy shop owner, not a SaaS user'*. Then *'find any word that sounds American where it should sound Indian'*. Three small asks beat one big ask, every time.

blocks.title: The classic trap: confusing well-read with experienced
blocks.md: Claude can quote Norman, Krug, Wroblewski. Claude cannot tell you whether the *Add to Cart* button on your screen is in the right place for your users. Reading a thousand books on swimming does not teach you to swim. The trap is treating Claude's authoritative tone as authority. The defense: every Claude design suggestion gets matched against either real user data or your own shipped experience. If neither exists, the suggestion is a hypothesis, not an answer.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Cookie-Cutter Mockup Pivot
blocks.source: Head of Design at Yodlee Studio, a Bengaluru product-design consultancy
blocks.story:
In late 2025, Yodlee's design team — 11 designers across 4 client engagements — ran a three-month experiment: ask Claude (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7) to *generate full mockups* for client work. *"We thought we'd 10x the throughput,"* the head of design wrote in a post-mortem. They did not 10x throughput.

What they got: **134 mockups across 9 weeks**, of which clients shipped **11**. The rest were polite-but-firm rejections: *"It looks like every other SaaS dashboard."* *"Where's the brand?"* *"This is a stock template."* The output was technically correct, hierarchically clean, and emotionally flat — what one client called *"the AI-generated airport-lounge of dashboards."*

In February 2026, the team switched modes. New rule: **Claude does not generate. Claude critiques.** A designer drafts, Claude reviews against a written brief, the designer iterates. Two-week loops, not one-shot generations. Three months later, the team's internal **design quality scores rose 37%** (measured on a rubric of brand fit, hierarchy, originality, accessibility), and client revision rounds dropped from an average of 4.2 to 1.8.

The head of design now runs a workshop titled *"Stop Asking Claude For Mockups."* It is fully booked.
blocks.takeaway: Generative-mode Claude in design produces the mean of its training data, which is the airport-lounge aesthetic. Critique-mode Claude makes your designer's work better. Same model, different verb.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Week 12 — Pitching the Design Lead
blocks.setup:
**Week 12 of Q2 2026.** The cowork rollout stuck. The CTO wants to expand Claude into the design team — **6 designers under Priya, Velora's design lead**. Priya is skeptical for the right reasons: she's seen the airport-lounge dashboards, she's read the Yodlee post-mortem, and she has zero patience for *"AI will speed you up"* pitches.

You — Karthik — get the 30-minute meeting. If you walk in pitching *"Claude generates mockups,"* Priya kills the rollout in the first five minutes. You need a workflow she'll actually adopt.

coach.name: Anthropic-Veteran Anuj
coach.role: Has personally pitched four skeptical design leads and lost two of them

stages.prompt: Anuj walks you in. *"What's the **one sentence** you open with?"*

options.label: "Claude can draft mockups in seconds — let me show you."
options.explain: Priya stands up and walks out before the demo loads. You opened with the *exact* claim Yodlee disproved over 9 weeks. You have lost the room.

options.label: "I'm not here to ask Claude to design. I'm here to ask Claude to be the loudest junior critic in your team."
options.explain: **This is the open.** Reframes Claude from *replacement* to *augmentation*, names the role specifically, and signals you've read Priya's objections before she had to raise them. She uncrosses her arms.

options.label: "Anthropic released a new design-system feature. Want a demo?"
options.explain: Feature-led pitches die in design rooms. Priya doesn't care what shipped; she cares what *changes about her team's work*. Lead with the workflow, not the product.

options.label: "Your designers spend 40% of their time on revisions. What if Claude pre-flagged the issues before client review?"
options.explain: **Strong.** Frames Claude as a *time-shift* tool, not a *replacement*. Numbers up front. Priya leans in to ask where the 40% came from.

stages.prompt: You have her attention. **What's the workflow you actually pitch?**

options.label: Designer drafts → Claude generates 3 alternative mockups → designer picks one.
options.explain: You just re-pitched the Yodlee experiment. Generative-mode Claude regresses to the mean. Priya recognizes the pattern instantly.

options.label: Designer drafts → Claude critiques against a written brief (brand, hierarchy, accessibility, edge cases) → designer iterates → repeat 2-3 times.
options.explain: **Exactly the Yodlee pivot.** Critique-mode is where Claude shines: it has read more design rubrics than any junior on Priya's team and won't get tired by round 4. The brief is the load-bearing artifact.

options.label: Claude reviews the entire Velora design system every Monday and posts 'inconsistencies' to Slack.
options.explain: Unsolicited weekly critique creates noise, not signal. Designers will mute the channel by week 3. Critique works *in the loop of a specific design*, not as a standing audit.

options.label: Designer drafts → Claude critiques → *and* Claude generates targeted alternatives for one specific element (e.g., 'just the empty-state illustration concept').
options.explain: **Top-tier.** Bounded generation on a specific micro-element is fine — it's the *whole-mockup generation* that fails. Priya is sketching this on her notepad.

stages.prompt: Priya pushes back: *"Where's the brief come from? My designers don't write briefs — they write Figma files."* **What's your move?**

options.label: "Claude can write the brief from the Figma file."
options.explain: If Claude writes the brief from the file it's about to critique, the critique becomes circular — Claude grading its own interpretation. The brief must come from a human source: client kickoff, design system, brand guide.

options.label: "We extract a 1-page brief from the existing client kickoff doc + Velora's brand guide. Reusable across projects. ~30 min one-time setup."
options.explain: **Right answer.** Briefs already exist as scattered artifacts; you're consolidating them. One-time setup, repeated value. Priya can see the math.

options.label: "We don't need a brief — Claude will figure it out from context."
options.explain: Without a brief, Claude critiques against generic best practices, which is exactly the airport-lounge problem in feedback form. The brief is what makes critique *Velora-specific*.

options.label: "The brief is a Claude Project — designers can re-use it across files, and it stays current as the brand evolves."
options.explain: **Even better.** Claude Projects make the brief a *living artifact* with persistent context. Designers don't re-paste it every session; the project carries it. This is the operational detail that makes the workflow stick.

stages.prompt: Priya is mostly sold. *"Fine — I'll pilot with **2 of my 6 designers** for one sprint. What's the success metric?"* **Pick one.**

options.label: "Number of mockups generated per week."
options.explain: Throughput-as-metric is exactly what produced the 134-to-11 Yodlee disaster. You're measuring the wrong thing on day one. Priya's hand is moving toward the meeting-end button.

options.label: "Client revision rounds per project. Baseline measured today, re-measured at end of sprint."
options.explain: **The right metric.** Yodlee saw 4.2 → 1.8 on this exact measure. It captures *quality of first delivery*, which is what critique-mode actually improves. Priya nods.

options.label: "Designer self-reported satisfaction with the workflow."
options.explain: Self-reported satisfaction will be glowing in week 1 (novelty) and lukewarm in week 4 (reality). Not a real signal. Use it as a tiebreaker, not the headline.

options.label: "Client revision rounds *and* designer hours per project, both measured against last quarter's baseline."
options.explain: **Top-tier.** Quality (revisions) + cost (hours) = the only two-axis measurement that catches both the airport-lounge failure mode *and* the 'critique takes longer than just doing the work' failure mode.

outcomes.perfect: You walked in with the right reframe, the right workflow, and the right metric. Priya is piloting with 2 designers, and if it works the other 4 follow naturally. **Anuj texts you afterward: 'You just saved us six months of design-team friction.'**
outcomes.good: You won the pitch but left some sharp edges (wrong metric, fuzzy brief sourcing). Re-read the lesson on **critique-mode vs. generative-mode** — getting the verb right is 80% of design rollouts.
outcomes.learn: You pitched the Yodlee experiment in a Velora meeting room. Priya killed it, the design team is now a no-go zone for AI rollout, and you've added 6 months of trust-rebuilding to your roadmap. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **Claude as critic, not generator** and **briefs as load-bearing artifacts**.

points: Claude is a junior designer who has read every book and shipped nothing — bring the taste, take the vocabulary.
Critique-not-generate: name the user, name the goal, name the primary action, ask for the 3 weakest decisions.
Iterative-tightening: 5 rounds with one constraint each beats 1 round with everything mashed together.
Claude does not generate images; use it to sharpen the brief and constrain a real image model's prompt.
Authoritative tone is not authority; every design suggestion is a hypothesis until matched against real user data.

lessons.title: Long-Running Workflows: Subagents, Background Jobs, Memory
lessons.subtitle: Break work into small bounded tasks; orchestrate the rest

blocks.md: Up to now, every Claude interaction in this course has been you and one Claude in a tight loop. This lesson is about the next level: workflows where multiple Claudes run in parallel, in the background, across hours, with handoffs between them. The word for this is **orchestration**, and it is where Claude either gets ten times more useful or ten times more wrong, with no middle ground. The teams that get orchestration right ship work that would take a 5-person team a week. The teams that get it wrong wake up to logs of a Claude run that touched 230 files based on an assumption it formed in step 4.

blocks.title: Mental model: Claude works best in small bounded tasks
blocks.md: A 4-hour Claude run is not 240 1-minute Claude runs in a row. It is 240 chances for context to drift, an assumption to harden, or an early mistake to compound. The mental model: **break every long workflow into small bounded tasks with explicit handoffs**. Each task knows its input, its scope, its expected output, and its hard stop. Each handoff is a small artifact a human or another agent can read in 60 seconds. This is exactly how you would run a real engineering team, and Claude responds to the same shape.

Junior ne run_in_background mein single job daala — 800 ITRs sequentially, ek context window mein. 6 ghante baad context overflow, partial results, kuch ITRs do baar process huye, kuch ek baar bhi nahi. Senior CA ne plan badla: **Haiku 4.5 batch API, parallel 50 at a time, har batch ek artifact likhe, fir orchestrator merge kare**. Same kaam 47 minute mein, 90% sasta. Lesson? Long sequential chains break. Bounded parallel batches scale.

en.title: Sequential is the enemy
en.md: A Pune CA firm tried to anomaly-check 800 ITRs in one sequential Claude run. Six hours later, half the ITRs were processed twice, half not at all, and the context had overflowed. Switching to Haiku 4.5 in batched parallel calls with one artifact per batch finished the same job in 47 minutes at one-tenth the cost.

blocks.md:
When you have a task that decomposes into N independent sub-tasks, do not run them in sequence. Fan out N subagents in parallel, each with a bounded brief, each writing a small artifact, and merge at the end. This is **the parallel fan-out pattern**, and it is the single biggest unlock once you understand orchestration.

The canonical example: investigating a slow build. A serial Claude would walk through the webpack config, then the test config, then the CI logs, then the dependency tree, taking 30 minutes and probably losing context by the end. A fan-out launches four `general-purpose` subagents at once, each with one focus area, each told to return a 5-bullet diagnosis with file references. Five minutes later you merge four artifacts and have the picture. The cost is roughly the same total tokens but the wall-clock is one-quarter and the quality is higher because no single agent's context got muddied.

When does fan-out *not* work? When the sub-tasks have dependencies — *'first figure out X, then use X to investigate Y'* is sequential by nature. The fan-out test: *'can these tasks run on different machines that never talk to each other and produce useful results?'* If yes, fan out. If no, sequence.

hi-IN.title: Mumbai local ka pattern
hi-IN.md: Bhai, Mumbai local mein 9 bogie hote hain, har bogie independently chalti hai par sab ek same destination pe pahunchti hain. Yahi fan-out hai. Agar 9 bogie ki jagah ek lambi train hoti, jisme har bogie pichhli ke saath physically locked rehti — to ek bogie atak gayi, sab atak jaate. Same with Claude. Independent subagents = parallel bogies. Locked sequential dependencies = ek lambi train, ek failure mein sab freeze.

en.title: Mumbai local as orchestration
en.md: Mumbai locals run nine independent coaches. One delay does not freeze the others; they all converge at the destination. That is fan-out. The opposite is a single locked train where one breakdown halts everything. Build your Claude workflows like the locals, not like a single articulated train.

blocks.md:
Long workflows fail because context dies. A 4-hour run accumulates 200K tokens of stdout, of which maybe 5K are signal and the rest is noise. The next step is operating on noise. The fix is the **artifact-handoff protocol**: every meaningful unit of work writes a small, structured artifact that the next unit reads instead of the raw stream.

What does an artifact look like? Concretely: a markdown file under 500 words with a fixed schema. For an investigation: *finding, evidence, location, severity, suggested next step*. For a code change: *files touched, summary diff, tests added, rollback*. For a data analysis: *question, method, top 3 results, caveats*. The next agent (or the next you) reads the artifact in 60 seconds and continues with high signal-to-noise.

Use this with `run_in_background` for long jobs. The background job writes the artifact at the end; your foreground agent reads only the artifact, never the 50K-line log. Use it across subagents in a fan-out. Use it across days when you pick up tomorrow what you started today. Use it when you hand off to a teammate. The artifact is the unit of agent work, exactly like a commit is the unit of human work.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the runaway loop
blocks.md: The single most expensive mistake in orchestration is **the runaway loop**: an agent that keeps going past its useful scope because the stop condition was vague. A loop told to *'fix the test failures'* with no scope might decide that fixing tests requires refactoring the test framework. Forty minutes later it has touched the test runner, the CI config and your package.json. Defenses: every loop needs a hard scope (*'only files matching tests/auth/**'*), a budget (*'stop after 8 tool calls'*), and a deliverable (*'write a 5-bullet summary at the end'*). Without all three, you are gambling.

en.title: The dabbawala protocol
en.md: The Mumbai dabbawalas run a 200K-meal-a-day system at 99.9% accuracy with no central computer. Each runner does one bounded leg; the tiffin tag is the artifact; the next runner trusts the tag without reading any history. That is exactly how to build Claude orchestration. Bounded leg, clear artifact, trusted handoff.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 200-File PR No One Could Review
blocks.source: Staff engineer at Vyapar Forge, a Hyderabad-based series-C developer-tooling company
blocks.story:
On a Friday in late March 2026, a Vyapar engineer kicked off an autonomous Claude Code run with a single prompt: *"Migrate our monolith from REST to gRPC. Take your time."* He gave it Opus 4.7 with the 1M-context window, MCP access to the repo, and went home for the weekend. He returned Monday to a **6-hour, 2.4M-token session** that had produced exactly what he asked for: a single PR, **207 files changed, +18,400 / -14,200 lines.**

It compiled. Most of the tests passed. It was, by any reasonable definition, the migration. It was also **completely unreviewable**. The senior engineer assigned the review opened the PR, scrolled for 90 seconds, closed the tab, and posted in #engineering: *"I cannot in good conscience approve this. Splitting it would take a week. Reviewing it line-by-line would take a month."*

The PR sat for 11 days. Eventually the team **closed it without merging** and rebuilt the migration from scratch using **bounded subagent tasks**: one service per subagent, ~15-30 file PRs, sequential merges, each reviewable in 30 minutes. Total elapsed time: 4 weeks. **Total reviewable PRs: 23.** Total merged: 23. Total trust intact.

The 6-hour autonomous run is now an in-house cautionary tale. Every Vyapar engineer who joins gets shown the screenshot of the closed PR.
blocks.takeaway: Long autonomous runs produce work, not reviewable work. Bounded subagents with tight artifacts are how you actually ship at scale — the constraint is *human review capacity*, not *model capacity*.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Week 14 — The TypeScript 6.0 Migration Fanout
blocks.setup:
**Week 14 of Q2 2026.** The Claude rollout is mostly stuck across Velora — coding, cowork, design. Last big task before quarter-end review: **migrate 14 microservices from TypeScript 5.4 to TypeScript 6.0.** Each service is 5k-40k lines, owned by 2-3 engineers, with non-trivial typing changes (the new `satisfies` semantics, narrowed `unknown`, stricter generic inference).

You — Karthik — have **two weeks**, **a budget of ~5M Claude tokens**, and a CTO who will personally read whatever ships. Get the design wrong and you produce a Vyapar-style 200-file disaster in 14 services at once.

coach.name: Anthropic-Veteran Anuj
coach.role: Has orchestrated three production migrations using subagent fanouts, two of which actually worked

stages.prompt: Anuj draws a whiteboard. *"First decision. **One big run, or many small ones?**"*

options.label: One big Opus 4.7 run, 1M-context, all 14 services in one session — the model can hold it all.
options.explain: This is exactly the Vyapar mistake at 14x scale. Even if the model can hold it, *humans cannot review it*. You'd produce one unreviewable PR per service, simultaneously. Disaster.

options.label: **14 parallel subagent tasks**, one per service, each with its own bounded `CLAUDE.md` and a 30-min-reviewable PR target.
options.explain: **Right architecture.** Subagents map cleanly to services. Reviewable-PR-as-constraint is the load-bearing rule. Anuj draws a green tick.

options.label: Sequential one-at-a-time runs across 14 services — safest, slowest.
options.explain: Sequential is *safer per task* but burns the entire two-week budget on serial latency. You have parallelism available; use it for the 11 services that don't share dependencies.

options.label: Parallel for the 11 independent services, **sequential for the 3 that share the auth library** (which itself needs migrating first).
options.explain: **Top-tier.** You correctly identified the dependency graph. Auth library migrates first (sequential), then 11 leaf services in parallel, then the 3 dependent services. This is the actual production-shaped plan.

stages.prompt: **Subagent design.** Each fanned-out task gets a prompt + context. **What goes in?**

options.label: *"Migrate this service to TypeScript 6.0."* + the repo path. That's it.
options.explain: No scope, no PR-size cap, no review hooks. The subagent will produce the Vyapar-shaped output: technically correct, operationally unmergeable.

options.label: Migration brief + service `CLAUDE.md` + an explicit **PR-size budget** ('split into PRs of ≤25 files; each must pass typecheck independently') + a **handoff artifact** (migration log written to `docs/MIGRATIONS/`).
options.explain: **This is the recipe.** PR-size budget enforces reviewability. Independent typecheck enforces incremental safety. The handoff artifact lets the next subagent (or human) pick up the thread without rerunning context.

options.label: Migration brief + a stern warning: 'Do not over-refactor.'
options.explain: Stern warnings without structural enforcement are decorative. The subagent needs *constraints*, not *requests*. PR-size budget is a constraint; 'don't over-refactor' is a hope.

options.label: Migration brief + service `CLAUDE.md` + PR-size budget + handoff artifact + **a checkpoint at each PR**: the subagent stops and waits for human approval before continuing.
options.explain: **Top-tier paranoia, correctly applied.** Checkpoints turn a 6-hour autonomous run into a 6-hour *supervised* run. You catch wrong-turn behavior at PR 1, not at PR 23.

stages.prompt: **Model picks.** You have Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, and Haiku 4.5 in the menu. **Which goes where?**

options.label: Opus 4.7 for everything — best model wins.
options.explain: You'd burn the 5M-token budget in 4 services and run dry. Opus is the right tool for *hard reasoning*, not for *applying a known migration to leaf code*.

options.label: **Opus 4.7** for the auth-library migration (hard, dependency-heavy, sets pattern). **Sonnet 4.6** for the 11 leaf services (apply known pattern). **Haiku 4.5** for repetitive cleanup (lint fixes, import reordering).
options.explain: **Exactly the cost-shape that works.** Reserve the most capable model for the load-bearing decision; let the cheaper models do the high-volume known work. This is how you stay inside 5M tokens.

options.label: Haiku 4.5 for everything — cheapest, fastest.
options.explain: Haiku will produce confidently-wrong type narrowing on the new `satisfies` semantics in three services. Cost-optimization without capability-matching is false economy.

options.label: Opus 4.7 for auth + the 3 dependent services. Sonnet 4.6 for the 11 leaves. **Skip Haiku** — too risky on type-system work.
options.explain: **Defensible.** TypeScript 6.0 type changes are subtle enough that you may not want Haiku in the loop at all. Higher per-token cost, but lower review burden. Anuj approves either of the two splits depending on team comfort.

stages.prompt: **Handoff design.** When a subagent finishes its service, what does it produce so the *next step* (human review, dependent-service subagent) can pick up cleanly?

options.label: Just the PR — the diff is the artifact.
options.explain: Diff-only handoffs lose the *reasoning*: why this approach over the alternative, what edge cases it punted on, what tests don't yet cover. Reviewers re-derive context that the subagent already had.

options.label: A `docs/MIGRATIONS/<service>.md` written by the subagent: scope, approach taken, decisions deferred, tests added, **known gaps**, suggested follow-up. Plus the PR.
options.explain: **The full handoff.** Reviewer reads the migration doc in 4 minutes, then reviews the PR in 25, total 30. Future engineer hitting an edge case 6 months later finds the 'known gaps' section. This is the artifact that makes the rollout *cumulative*.

options.label: PR + a Slack message in #engineering summarizing what the subagent did.
options.explain: Slack messages are ephemeral. In 6 weeks the channel will have scrolled past, and the migration context will live nowhere durable. Use docs, not chat.

options.label: Handoff doc + PR + **automated checkpoint**: the next dependent-service subagent reads the upstream service's migration doc as part of its context window.
options.explain: **Top-tier.** This is the orchestration pattern that compounds: each subagent builds on the last one's *learnings*, not just its *output*. By service 14, you've encoded 13 services' worth of edge cases.

outcomes.perfect: You designed a real production fanout: dependency-aware ordering, model-tier matching, PR-size budgets, handoff artifacts, and checkpoints. **23 reviewable PRs land in two weeks**, the CTO reads three of them and stops there because they're boring in the best way. Velora's Q2 review goes well. **Anuj quietly forwards your design doc to the Anthropic team as a customer reference.**
outcomes.good: You got the architecture mostly right but cut a corner on either model selection or handoff design. Re-read the lesson on **bounded subagents** — the difference between 23 reviewable PRs and 1 Vyapar PR is in the artifacts, not the model.
outcomes.learn: You either built one giant unreviewable run, or you parallelized without thinking through dependencies and produced 14 conflicting PRs. Re-read the lesson — especially the sections on **PR-size budgets**, **dependency-aware fanout**, and **handoff artifacts**. The constraint is human review capacity, always.

points: Long unsupervised Claude loops drift; break work into small bounded tasks with explicit handoffs.
Parallel fan-out: independent sub-tasks run in parallel subagents, merge at the end. One-quarter wall clock, higher quality.
Artifact handoff: every agent writes a 500-word structured deliverable. The next agent reads only the artifact, never the stream.
Every long-running brief needs three constraints: scope, budget, deliverable. Without them you are gambling.
MCP and tool integrations expand power and risk together; never combine two unsafe capabilities without a human review gate.
